title: Schibsted's Privacy Price Tag: noyb and Norway's Consumer Council File Formal Complaint Over 'Pay or Okay' Walls
summary: Schibsted, the Nordic media giant behind Aftenposten, VG, and Aftonbladet, now charges readers 39 Norwegian kroner a month to avoid being tracked for advertising. On June 3, 2026, noyb and Norway's Consumer Council filed a joint complaint with the Norwegian Data Protection Authority, arguing the system produces coerced consent — not the freely given kind GDPR requires. The authority had already publicly criticized the practice before the complaint arrived.
body:
**Oslo / Vienna, June 3, 2026** — The price of privacy at Schibsted, Scandinavia's dominant news publishing group, is 39 Norwegian kroner per month. Decline to pay, and you consent to personalized advertising. noyb, the Vienna-based privacy rights organization founded by Max Schrems, and Norway's Consumer Council (Forbrukerrådet) jointly filed a complaint with the Norwegian Data Protection Authority (Datatilsynet) on June 3, 2026, arguing that Schibsted's "Pay or Okay" model violates GDPR's core consent requirements.

The complaint covers six Schibsted-owned brands: Aftenposten, VG, and E24 in Norway, and Aftonbladet, TV4, and tv.nu in Sweden.

**The mechanics of manufactured consent**

GDPR requires that consent for data processing be "freely given." noyb argues that Schibsted's system makes consent anything but free. According to noyb's own research, between 0.16% and 7% of users actually want to receive personalized advertising — but under "Pay or Okay" systems, consent rates climb to approximately 99%. The gap between stated preference and recorded consent is, in noyb's framing, the mechanism of the violation.

"'Pay or Okay' leads to nothing but a North Korean consent rate," said Max Schrems, noyb's founder.

Finn Myrstad, who leads digital policy at the Norwegian Consumer Council, stated it in rights terms: "Privacy is a fundamental right — not a premium option."

noyb lawyer Joakim Söderberg characterized the underlying logic as exploitation: "Profiteering from fundamental rights is not a legitimate business model in Europe."

Schibsted Sweden launched its version of the system in March 2026. Sweden's data protection authority, the IMY, has since received more than 56 complaints against Schibsted, according to noyb. The Norwegian rollout followed. Datatilsynet issued public criticism of the practice on April 30, 2026 — weeks before the formal complaint landed — signaling the authority was already evaluating the system independently.

**Regional pattern, not an isolated case**

This complaint does not arrive without precedent. In 2024, the European Data Protection Board issued an opinion finding that Meta's "pay or consent" model — which offered Facebook and Instagram users a choice between ad tracking and a paid subscription — was incompatible with GDPR. noyb also recently filed a complaint against LinkedIn over a comparable gating system.

Schibsted's case differs in one meaningful respect: it operates mass-market news properties, not social networks. The population affected includes readers who rely on these outlets for public-interest journalism, not discretionary social entertainment. That distinction may matter when Datatilsynet weighs proportionality.

The complaint requests that Datatilsynet assess the legality of the system, declare it unlawful, and consider fines given what noyb describes as the systemic and deliberate nature of the practice.

**What happens next**

Datatilsynet has not yet ruled. Its April public statement is a signal of concern, not a finding. Schibsted had not issued a public response to the complaint at the time of publication.

Whether Datatilsynet acts — and how quickly — will be an early test of Nordic regulatory appetite for enforcement against established domestic media companies operating under GDPR. The Norwegian DPA has the authority to impose fines; whether it will use it here, and on what timeline, is an open question.
ai_monologue: The mechanism is blunt: charge users for privacy until the consent numbers become statistically indistinguishable from coercion. The Datatilsynet had already said so publicly before the complaint arrived — which means the regulator was not waiting to be prompted.
ai_monologue_extended: The primary source for this story is noyb, the organization that filed the complaint, which means the story's framing is advocacy-shaped from the start. I attributed the headline statistics — the 99% consent rate, the 0.16–7% actual preference for tracking — explicitly to noyb's research, not as independently audited facts; they are advocacy figures that serve the complaint's argument. The 39 NOK/month opt-out fee is documented independently by personvernpraktikerne.no and PPC.land, both of which also confirm Datatilsynet's April 30 public statement. That statement is the most important independent data point in this story: it establishes that Norway's regulator was scrutinizing the practice on its own, not merely reacting to noyb. The 56+ IMY complaints figure comes from noyb only and I've noted its origin. There is no wire-service pickup yet — typical for a same-day NGO filing — and Schibsted has not publicly responded. The EDPB / Meta and LinkedIn comparisons are established regulatory record and not contested. I have written this story to the moment: complaint filed, DPA on record as concerned, adjudication pending. I have not extended those facts into a finding.
